items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider a circle with center [MATH: O] and two distinct points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] on the circumference.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f9c15865b45fb47cac624c0a81a62067]

Content:
Recall that the points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] determine two distinct arcs on the circle:

Content:
- The minor arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] consists of [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] and all points on the circle that lie inside [MATH: \angle AOB.]
- The major arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] consists of [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] and all points on the circle that lie outside [MATH: \angle AOB.]

Content:
Let's refer to the following diagram, where [MATH: m\angle AOB = 80^\circ.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/105e4cdce7483bf988ae4526a76f7885]

Content:
Here, [MATH: \angle AOB] is called the central angle corresponding to the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}.]

Content:
In general, a minor arc is said to have the same measure as its central angle. Here, the minor arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] has the central angle [MATH: \angle AOB.] Therefore, the measure of the arc is
[MATH: mAB^(⌢)|= m∠AOB = 80^{∘}.]

Content:
Now, since there are [MATH: 360^\circ] in a full circle, the major arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] must have a measure of
[MATH: mACB^(⌢)|= 360^{∘} − m∠AOB; = 360^{∘} − 80^{∘}; = 280^{∘}.]

Content:
Labeling the measures of the arcs without explicitly labeling the central angle is common. For example:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/baafc6a338c57893702f0c67efa76b3d]

Content:
Note: When we use arc notation with only two letters (e.g., [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}]), this always refers to the minor arc.

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the diagram above. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ AB }] is equal to [MATH: 100^\circ]

  2. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is equal to [MATH: 240^\circ]

  3. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is equal to [MATH: 120^\circ]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/dd358374fcc9bf213a843ac563868bd6]

Consider the diagram above. Which of the following statements are true?

1. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ AB }] is equal to [MATH: 100^\circ]
2. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is equal to [MATH: 240^\circ]
3. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is equal to [MATH: 120^\circ]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine the statements one by one.

  • Statement I is false. The measure of the minor arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] is equal to the measure of its central angle, [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{AB} = m\angle{AOB}=120^\circ.]

  • Statement II is true, while statement III is false. The arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] represents the major arc of the circle, so it has the measure [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{ACB} = 360^\circ - m\angle{AOB} =360^\circ - 120^\circ =240^\circ.]

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

items.title: Determining Measures of Central Angles

sections.normalized_html: What is the measure, in degrees, of the central angle corresponding to the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{BC}?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/428e7eb45028bd7886b2da4d3a9d8b72]

What is the measure, in degrees, of the central angle corresponding to the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{BC}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
When an arc notation contains only two letters, it is always assumed to be a minor arc.

So here, [MATH: \overset{\frown}{BC}] represents the minor arc of the circle with the central angle [MATH: \angle{BOC}.]

Therefore, its measure is

[MATH: mBC^(⌢)|= m∠BOC; = m∠AOB + m∠AOC; = 90^{∘} + 45^{∘}; = 135^{∘}.]

sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/258edd37a33484ef0143354a983220d6]

Given that [MATH: m\angle{DOA}=125^\circ], [MATH: m\angle{AOB} = 95^\circ] and [MATH: m\angle{COD}=90^\circ,] find the measure of [MATH: \angle{AOC}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that [MATH: m\angle COD = 90^\circ] and [MATH: m\angle AOC = m\angle AOB + m\angle BOC.]

Since all the angles in the diagram together make a full circle of [MATH: 360^\circ,] we have

[MATH: m∠DOA + (m∠AOB + m∠BOC) + m∠COD|= 360^{∘}; 125^{∘} + m∠AOC + 90^{∘}|= 360^{∘}; 215^{∘} + m∠AOC|= 360^{∘}; m∠AOC|= 145^{∘}.]

In the diagram above, [MATH: \overline{AD},] [MATH: \overline{BE},] and [MATH: \overline{CF}] are diameters. If [MATH: m\angle{AOF=50^\circ}] and [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{BC}=3x-10^\circ,] then what is the value of [MATH: x?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
From the diagram,

[MATH: m\angle{EOD} = m\angle{AOF} = 50^\circ.]

Since the measures of [MATH: \angle{AOF},] [MATH: \angle{FOE}] and [MATH: \angle{EOD},] add up to [MATH: 180^\circ,] we have

[MATH: m∠AOF + m∠FOE + m∠EOD|= 180^{∘}; 50^{∘} + m∠FOE + 50^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 100^{∘} + m∠FOE|= 180^{∘}; m∠FOE|= 80^{∘}.]

Now, since the angles [MATH: \angle{FOE}] and [MATH: \angle{BOC}] are vertical, we obtain [MATH: m\angle{BOC} = m\angle{FOE} = 80^\circ.]

Finally, since the measure of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{BC}] is equal to the measure of the central angle [MATH: \angle{BOC},] we have

[MATH: BC^(⌢)|= m∠BOC; 3x − 10^{∘}|= m∠BOC; 3x − 10^{∘}|= 80^{∘}; 3x|= 90^{∘}; x|= 30^{∘}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's consider a circle with center [MATH: O] and two distinct points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] on the circumference.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f9c15865b45fb47cac624c0a81a62067]

Content:
Recall that the points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] determine two distinct arcs on the circle:

Content:
- The minor arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] consists of [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] and all points on the circle that lie inside [MATH: \angle AOB.]
- The major arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] consists of [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] and all points on the circle that lie outside [MATH: \angle AOB.]

Content:
Let's refer to the following diagram, where [MATH: m\angle AOB = 80^\circ.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/105e4cdce7483bf988ae4526a76f7885]

Content:
Here, [MATH: \angle AOB] is called the central angle corresponding to the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}.]

Content:
In general, a minor arc is said to have the same measure as its central angle. Here, the minor arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] has the central angle [MATH: \angle AOB.] Therefore, the measure of the arc is
[MATH: mAB^(⌢)|= m∠AOB = 80^{∘}.]

Content:
Now, since there are [MATH: 360^\circ] in a full circle, the major arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] must have a measure of
[MATH: mACB^(⌢)|= 360^{∘} − m∠AOB; = 360^{∘} − 80^{∘}; = 280^{∘}.]

Content:
Labeling the measures of the arcs without explicitly labeling the central angle is common. For example:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/baafc6a338c57893702f0c67efa76b3d]

Content:
Note: When we use arc notation with only two letters (e.g., [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}]), this always refers to the minor arc.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying True Statements About Central Angles

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/dd358374fcc9bf213a843ac563868bd6]

Consider the diagram above. Which of the following statements are true?

1. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ AB }] is equal to [MATH: 100^\circ]
2. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is equal to [MATH: 240^\circ]
3. The measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is equal to [MATH: 120^\circ]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. The measure of the minor arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] is equal to the measure of its central angle,
[MATH: m\overset{\frown}{AB} = m\angle{AOB}=120^\circ.]
- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. The arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] represents the major arc of the circle, so it has the measure
[MATH: m\overset{\frown}{ACB} = 360^\circ - m\angle{AOB} =360^\circ - 120^\circ =240^\circ.]

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

Item 5 — Example: Determining Measures of Central Angles

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/428e7eb45028bd7886b2da4d3a9d8b72]

What is the measure, in degrees, of the central angle corresponding to the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{BC}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
When an arc notation contains only two letters, it is always assumed to be a minor arc.

So here, [MATH: \overset{\frown}{BC}] represents the minor arc of the circle with the central angle [MATH: \angle{BOC}.]

Therefore, its measure is

[MATH: mBC^(⌢)|= m∠BOC; = m∠AOB + m∠AOC; = 90^{∘} + 45^{∘}; = 135^{∘}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that [MATH: m\angle COD = 90^\circ] and [MATH: m\angle AOC = m\angle AOB + m\angle BOC.]

Since all the angles in the diagram together make a full circle of [MATH: 360^\circ,] we have

[MATH: m∠DOA + (m∠AOB + m∠BOC) + m∠COD|= 360^{∘}; 125^{∘} + m∠AOC + 90^{∘}|= 360^{∘}; 215^{∘} + m∠AOC|= 360^{∘}; m∠AOC|= 145^{∘}.]

Item 11 — Example: Finding an Unknown Using Central Angles

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/753e47ac2ee0f174a8a210561044246c]

In the diagram above, [MATH: \overline{AD},] [MATH: \overline{BE},] and [MATH: \overline{CF}] are diameters. If [MATH: m\angle{AOF=50^\circ}] and [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{BC}=3x-10^\circ,] then what is the value of [MATH: x?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
From the diagram,

[MATH: m\angle{EOD} = m\angle{AOF} = 50^\circ.]

Since the measures of [MATH: \angle{AOF},] [MATH: \angle{FOE}] and [MATH: \angle{EOD},] add up to [MATH: 180^\circ,] we have

[MATH: m∠AOF + m∠FOE + m∠EOD|= 180^{∘}; 50^{∘} + m∠FOE + 50^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 100^{∘} + m∠FOE|= 180^{∘}; m∠FOE|= 80^{∘}.]

Now, since the angles [MATH: \angle{FOE}] and [MATH: \angle{BOC}] are vertical, we obtain
[MATH: m\angle{BOC} = m\angle{FOE} = 80^\circ.]

Finally, since the measure of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{BC}] is equal to the measure of the central angle [MATH: \angle{BOC},] we have

[MATH: BC^(⌢)|= m∠BOC; 3x − 10^{∘}|= m∠BOC; 3x − 10^{∘}|= 80^{∘}; 3x|= 90^{∘}; x|= 30^{∘}.]
